chapter_theme: Songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 3 of 5), many sung at its towers (கோபுரம்): the poet confesses to women who demand money, plunder and cheat, catalogues the body and its diseases, imagines his death and cremation, and asks for the feet, wisdom and the company of devotees; the praise turns on Siva's dance at Puliyur, Murugan as Siva's teacher, and the gopurams of the temple.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (479, 481 to 484, 486, 489, 491, 492); the body and its diseases (480, 485, 487); death and cremation (490) and countless births (493); and an akam song in the voice of a lovesick girl's companion (488). The towers are named: south (480), west (481 to 484), north (485), all four (486).

479.reading: The poet describes women who grab a man's side, press shoulder to shoulder, bite his lips, loosen their ornaments, say 'give money', wink and talk, coax with feigned love and then pick quarrels, and calls himself the fool who wanders in the blame of these tricksters; he asks for grace to reach the supreme and Murugan's feet. The praise shows Murugan crushing the Suras with a club, Devayanai on a golden couch and Valli of the millet field, and Siva who danced to the drum's beat beyond the knowing of Brahma and Vishnu, at the tower of the Tiruchitrambalam.
479.nuance: தாபணமே என: the women's demand for money is quoted in their own words. பசப்பிப் பின் பிணக்கைக் கூறிய: feigned love followed by the made-up quarrel is the courtesan's way of ending a spent man's welcome. The plea's last words (பரத்துற் றண்பதத்துப் போதக் மீதென) are garbled.

480.reading: The poet calls the body a hut of bone, rheum, marrow, brain, phlegm, water, hair and skin, crammed with pus, worms and flesh, its nerves like tubes, where the tricksters of the senses dwell; he says the desires for women and for land, with evil and fated deeds and time, have gathered in it, and asks not to spread in sorrow but to be given the feet that rise to the release of Sadasiva and the supreme world. The praise shows the battle in drum syllables, the Suras drowned with their chariots and horses as food for the vel, Siva dancing, and Murugan on the peacock with Valli at the southern tower.
480.nuance: ஆசை பெணாசை மணாசைகள்: the familiar triad of cravings (woman, land, gold) appears with gold folded into ஆசை. தீவினை ஊழ்வினை காலமொடு: deed, fated deed and time are named together as the forces that keep him in sorrow.

481.reading: The poet describes women whose breasts are like elephants ready for war, with hearts as dry as the cane waste from the mill, who seem like lovers while thinking only of whose wealth they can take, and whose long eyes are a net like the spears of Death's messengers; he asks for grace not to be joined in lust with these tricksters who cast down the lustful drowned in love's sea. The praise shows Murugan as a lion against the Suras on the blue peacock, Vishnu who shot Ravana's crowns as his uncle, and Brahma and the gods worshipping at the western tower in Puliyur.
481.nuance: ஆலைக் கோதினில் ஈரமிலா மனம்: their hearts have no more moisture than the crushed cane thrown from the mill. ஆருக்கே பொருளாம் என நினைவதனாலே: their thought is only whose money it will be. The eyes are காலத் தூதர் கை வேல், Death's messengers' spears, so the courtesan and Death are drawn together.

482.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes reach to the ears and wound like carp, with cloud-dark hair, who play proudly in the shade of groves and stir lust that heeds no counsel, and asks to be given the path that escapes the burning evil of drowning in their breasts. The praise shows Murugan walking through the hunters' forest for love of Valli until his fragrant feet reddened, cutting down Sura who hid in the sea, and Puliyur where the dust of chariots in the streets hides the sun's chariot, at the western tower praised by learned Vedic priests.
482.nuance: வாசத் தாள் சிவப்ப வருவோனே: the god's feet redden from walking to Valli, a tender picture against the battle praise. கேள்வி அற்ற காமப் பூசல்: lust is a quarrel deaf to instruction.

483.reading: The poet lists women: greedy plunderers, skilled deceivers, collectors who take a toll, killers with their eyes, gamblers in speech, coral-lipped and cruel, who pain the heart while seeming close and hide enmity within, and asks that he, a dog wandering in maya, be saved by Murugan coming with golden shoulders, twelve hands, the kadamba garland and six faces, and giving inner wisdom. The praise shows the vel thrown at Taraka, Rama whose golden foot turned a stone into a fair form as he went to the forest, Devayanai joined as promised, and Valli, at the western tower of Thillai.
483.nuance: சூறைகள் கொள்ளும் ஆயக்காரிகள்: the women are toll collectors who plunder, a picture of love as a tax. கல்லிலே பொற்றாள் படவே அது நல்ல ரூபத்தே வர: the stone that became a woman at Rama's touch is Ahalya, named only by the deed.

484.reading: The poet lists the arts by which women give infatuation, flowered hair, anklet feet, rhythm of hands, sly talk, scented smiles, contrary speech, swan gait, breasts and their cloth, and their haughty price in coin, and says he sinks daily in their sea of lust; he asks for grace to join Murugan's devotees, the silent jnanis. The praise names Vishnu who came when the elephant cried 'root of the four Vedas' as his uncle, Sivakami as his mother, the three thousand Vedic priests of Puliyur who worship daily by sacrifice, and Murugan on the peacock at the western tower, tall as Meru.
484.nuance: The plea's remedy is company: மோன ஞானிகளுடனே சேரவும், to join the silent knowers. மேன்மை மூவாயிர வேதியர்: the three thousand Brahmins of Thillai, the temple's hereditary priests. The elephant's cry is the Gajendra story, as in 25.

485.reading: The poet catalogues the body, bone, skin, hair, nerves, pus, worms, brain, a sea of blood, a pot of filth, and its diseases, fatigue, anaemia, wind, rib pain, colic, asthma, hernia, fever, diabetes, phlegm, deafness, hunchback, cholera, blindness, lameness, dumbness and scrofula, and confesses that, taking this flawed dwelling as permanent, he wanders by ruinous deeds; he asks for the feet, wisdom and love. The praise names the Goddess who rides the old golden bull, Siva who pressed Ravana down under his foot when he lifted the mountain, and Valli, at the northern tower in Puliyur.
485.nuance: குடிப்புக்கு ஊனம் இதே சதமாம் என எடுத்து: the fault is not having a diseased body but taking it for a lasting home. Siva's name is given in the five syllables (சிவாயநமோ).

486.reading: The poet describes women with dark hair, swinging earrings, dancing ornaments and ringing anklets, who walk like peacocks and speak words sweet as milk, women for a price, and calls himself the fool who, loving them, drowns in ruinous deeds and sinks into the seven hells; he asks for Siva's son's feet. The praise shows Murugan on the peacock with the vel, the seas and islands shaken and the asuras reduced to rubbish, Uma, Vishnu's sister who never leaves Siva's side, and Murugan with Devayanai at the four towers of Puliyur, land of wisdom.
486.nuance: விலைமாதர்: the women are named by their price. ஞான பூமியதான பேர்புலியூர்: Chidambaram is called the land of wisdom. The plea's last line (காரிர் பாருமை யாசி வாபத) is garbled.

487.reading: The poet lists the body's diseases, wind, bile, colic, abscess, stone, phlegm, cough, scrofula, blindness, deafness, dumbness, piles and dropsy, calls it a body eaten by the ninety-six tattvas, and confesses wandering in many guises, gripped by the poison of desire for wealth; he asks whether, instead of building houses, falling into infatuation and dying with his voice gone, his mind will not think of the pure space where the peacock dances, which gives release. The praise names Siva of the five syllables, helper of pure devotees, with green Uma, as Murugan's father, Murugan as the younger brother of Vinayaka who taught the supreme one the primal meaning, and the lord of Valli at the golden crystal tower of Puliyur.
487.nuance: தொண்ணூற்றாறு தத்துவர்கள் உண்ட காயம்: the ninety-six tattvas are pictured as eaters of the body. மயிலாடு சுத்தவெளி: release is a pure space where the peacock dances, the Lord's vehicle become the image of the goal. பரப்பிரமன் ஆதி உற்ற பொருள் ஓதுவித்த: the Om story, with Siva as the supreme one taught, though the phrase may be divided otherwise.

488.reading: In the voice of a lovesick girl's companion or mother, the singer says the girl, an innocent doe, is ruined by the cuckoos calling in every grove, the cold north wind, Kama's fragrant arrows, the gossip of women who follow her, the flower bed and the bell of the returning bull, and asks Murugan, knowing her plight, to give her his honeyed garland. The praise shows the elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms, Siva who dances in the hall at Perumpatrappuliyur among cane fields, Murugan who comes on the peacock to end devotees' sorrow, and the vel that rolled Sura over.
488.nuance: This is akam poetry with no confession of the poet's own: the signs of evening (the bull's bell, the cold wind) and the women's gossip (மாதர் வசை) are classical. The garland asked for (மது மாலை) is the lover's token that would make the love public.

489.reading: The poet describes women who talk with milk-sweet words, play at pleasure, are skilled in schemes and wind in money with their tricks, and will not call a man back unless he pays what they name, and asks that, rather than enjoying them, falling into evil and great hell and becoming a corpse, he grasp Murugan's feet and speak his praise. The praise names Vishnu who cut Ravana's ten heads as his uncle, the vel that killed Surapadman's clan, the battlefield where vultures and ghouls tear corpses, and Murugan on the peacock at Perumpatrappuliyur, where jnanis seek his anklet feet.
489.nuance: பலஞ் செப்பித் தர மீள அழையாதவர்: they call a man back only if he pays the sum they name. The plea sets two ends side by side: becoming a corpse in hell (நரகடைந்திட்டுச் சவமாகி) or holding the feet and speaking praise.

490.reading: The poet imagines the day his life departs: held captive by the buffalo-rider Death, the pleasures desired through women's eyes and the wisdom and honour he spoke of all become mere water and empty space, his body lies as food for the pyre, kin wail and carry it to the burning ground; he asks that before then Murugan grant whichever of two gains is fitting, the goal won by dying in the mind, or understanding won by living on. The praise tells of Rama, who shook the seven sal trees, killed Vali, saw Lanka burned and cut down Ravana's crowns, as Murugan's uncle, and hails Murugan as the one poet for the world, the crest-jewel of the Saiva Veda and lord of its hymns, at Perumpatrappuliyur.
490.nuance: மனதாலே இறந்திட்டுப் பெறவே கதியாயினும் இருந்திட்டுப் பெறவே மதியாயினும்: the poet leaves to the Lord the choice between dying to the world in mind and living on to gain understanding. ப்ரபஞ்சத்துக்கொரு பாவலனார் ... சிவ வேத சிகாமணி ப்ரபந்தத்துக்கொரு நாத: the titles fit Sambandar, the Thevaram poet, so Murugan seems identified with him.

491.reading: The poet describes women with swinging earrings, conch-white smiles, cloud hair, carp-arrow eyes and cuckoo voices, snatchers of gold who come with tricks, talk with betel-red mouths, name their wage and then sport on the bed, and asks Murugan to end his act of handing his goods to them. The praise names Siva who took Death's life, burned the three cities and Kama's body, felled Daksha, the sun and moon, and dances in the hall, and Murugan as that Siva's guru, the vel against Surapadman, and Valli, at Puliyur.
491.nuance: சம்பளம் ஈது என ஓதி: the women state their wage, love priced as hired work. தன் குருநாதா: Murugan is the guru of the very Siva whose deeds the praise lists. மூளியர் may mean women stripped of ornaments, or be abuse.

492.reading: The poet names women as cheats in every way, by smile, betel mouth, shamelessness, eyes, sore-ridden thighs, gait, breasts, speech, hair and song, who gather and dance through the streets, and asks that Murugan, by his own act, give the anklet of wondrous wisdom to him, a dog who wanders with them. The praise shows the vel that broke the hill and the serpent's hoods, Murugan as the teacher who lovingly taught the truth to Siva, partner of Sivakami, giving his servant the sea of the bliss of wisdom, and his secret love for Valli, at Puliyur.
492.nuance: எத்திகள், cheats, ends every phrase of the first half, a rhetorical list like 470's. சத்துப தேசிக்குங் குரவோனே: Murugan as Siva's teacher of the Real. உன் செயலால்: the wisdom is to come by the Lord's act, not the poet's effort.

493.reading: The poet says his births are more than the sands of the seven seas if counted, that now his life and body are Murugan's charge and he can no longer leave a body, that vultures, jackals, fire, earth, Yama and Brahma are all worn out with him, and that protection is Murugan's duty and this servant is his servant, so let him quickly give his feet. The praise names Uma, emerald-formed and pure, as Murugan's mother, the peacock that shakes the mountains, the vel that feeds on asura lives, and the dance at Puliyur praised by gods and sages.
493.nuance: கழுகொடு நரியும் எரி புவி மறலி கமலனும் மிகவும் அயர்வானார்: those who receive each body (vultures and jackals, fire and earth), the god who takes it (Yama) and the god who makes the next (Brahma) are all exhausted by his countless births, a wry turn. கடன் உனது அபயம்: refuge is the Lord's debt. இனியுடல் விடுக முடியாது may also mean he cannot bear to give up a body again.

links.note: Both join the catalogue of the body's diseases to the ninety-six tattvas living off the body; 487 adds the house-building and desire for wealth that keep the poet from the space where the peacock dances.
Tirumular counts the ninety-six as tenants of a walled temple who run off when it falls; 487 makes the same ninety-six the eaters of the body, a picture of consumption rather than desertion.
Both turn the body into a dwelling whose real occupants are diseases, listed at length; 485 names the fault as taking that dwelling for permanent.

Tirumular's Siva-jnanis go about as dead while their senses and body remain; 490 asks for exactly this, the goal won by dying in the mind before the body is carried to the burning ground, but offers the Lord the alternative of living on in understanding.

The Naladiyar says it matters nothing whether the body is dragged, buried or thrown away once its dweller has left; 493 lists the same receivers of the corpse, vultures, jackals, fire and earth, but as weary claimants, so that the repetition across countless births is itself the burden.

Both are laments for a girl sick with love for Murugan, told by another voice, with the wind, the birds and the signs of evening wearing her down; 24 is the mother's, and 488 asks Murugan for his garland.

Both make the courtesan's only question whose money there is: the Naladiyar's women find even an oil-presser sweet if he has wealth, and 481's women, with hearts dry as cane waste, think only whose wealth it will be.

The song's women coax with feigned love and then pick a quarrel (பசப்பிப் பின் பிணக்கைக் கூறிய வீணிகள்) once the money is asked and given. The Naladiyar's women seem sweet while a man is infatuated and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாம் ஆர்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்), and those who would reach the right path avoid them. Both mark the same turn from coaxing to coldness; the Naladiyar ties it to the path, the song to the plea for the feet.

The song makes the body a walled hut where the tricksters of the senses (பொறி விரகாளர்) dwell and where craving for women and land gathers (ஆசை பெணாசை மணாசைகள் தொக்கு), and asks for release. The Naladiyar names the five senses as five mouths of craving (ஐவாய வேட்கை அவா) and promises release to one who can guard them. The song confesses that it cannot do this guarding and asks the Lord for the release the Naladiyar ties to it.

The song calls the women's long eyes a net like the spears in the hands of Death's messengers (காலத் தூதர் கை வேலெனு நீள்விழி). The Kural's lover asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both draw the woman's look and Death together; in the Kural it is the lover's wonder, in the song a warning against the trade.

The song's praise shows Murugan walking through the hunters' forest for love of Valli until his fragrant feet reddened (வேடக் கானகத்து வாசத்தாள் சிவப்ப வருவோனே). The Naladiyar's mother asks whether her daughter's feet, which drew back even from red dye on soft cotton, have borne the stony forest path (பரற்கானம்) of her elopement. Both measure love by tender feet on the wild path; the song gives the god the part of the eloping lover.

The song's women pain the heart while seeming close and hide enmity within (உள்ள நோவைத்தே உறவாடியர் ... உள்விரோதக்காரிகள்). The Naladiyar's women keep a heart that does harm hidden inside (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் தம் உள்ளடக்கி) and speak words to be trusted, yet belong to no one but their bodies. Both locate the deceit in the concealed heart behind the closeness.

Sinking daily in the sea of lust the women give, the song asks for its remedy in company: to join the Lord's devotees, the silent jnanis (உனது அடியாராகிய மோன ஞானிகளுடனே சேரவும்). The Kural says there is no greater support than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more trouble than bad. The song applies the Kural's rule to the spiritual life, setting the devotees against the women.

The song catalogues the body's filth and diseases and names the fault as taking this flawed dwelling for lasting (குடிப்புக்கு ஊனம் இதே சதமாம் என). Tirumular addresses those who feel that the hut that does not stay is permanent (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்) and says the Lord cannot be seen in their hearts. Both make the error not the body's frailty but the belief in its permanence.

The song calls itself the fool who, loving women for a price (விலைமாதர்), drowns in ruinous deeds and sinks into the seven hells (ஏழ்நரகு ஆழும் மூடனை). The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who set no limit the அளறு, hell and mire at once, in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). The shared verb ஆழ் shows the song taking the Kural's hell literally and multiplying it to seven.

Among the things that torment the lovesick girl the song names the bell of the bull coming home at evening (அடைந்திட்ட விடைமேவு மணியாலும). The Kural's woman calls the herdsman's flute a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the gentle pastoral sound of the herds' return into evening's weapon against the parted lover.

The song's women will not call a man back unless he pays the sum they name (பலஞ் செப்பித் தர மீள அழையாதவர்). The Naladiyar says that even if he were Mal whom the gods worship, they would dismiss with joined hands a man with nothing to give (கொடுப்பதொன்றில்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). Both make payment the only thing that keeps a man welcome; the Naladiyar's god makes the point by exaggeration.

The song's women talk with betel-red mouths, play at intimacy and state their wage (சம்பளம் ஈது என ஓதி) before the bed. The Kural says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the sweet talk ending in the named wage, the motive the Kural names.

The song names women cheats (எத்திகள்) in every part and act and asks, as a dog wandering with them, for the anklet of wondrous wisdom by the Lord's own act (உன் செயலால் அற்புத ஞானத்தின் கழல்). The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an அணங்கு to those without discerning understanding. The song accepts the Kural's diagnosis, lack of understanding, and asks for the wisdom from the Lord rather than from his own effort.

The song counts births beyond the sands of the seven seas and says the servant is the Lord's servant (அடிமை உன் அடிமை), so his protection is the Lord's debt (கடன் உனது அபயம்). Tirumular says a deed of servitude to Siva (ஆவணம்) was written for him, his mother and father across seven times seven births. The song presses the bond Tirumular records as a legal claim on the Lord.

source_issues: Song 486: one corrupt character in காலினு஡புர (line 7), probably காலின் நூபுர, 'the anklets of the feet', with ஡ for ஊ; also the unflagged garbles காரிர் பாருமை யாசி வாபத (line 12) and யீண (line 20).
Song 487: one corrupt character in புற்றெழுதலு஡சல் (line 3), probably ஊசல், with ஡ for ஊ.
Song 492: unflagged garbles சிவகா மிககொரு (line 17, probably சிவகாமிக்கு ஒரு) and சுக்முழ் கி (line 24, probably சுகம் மூழ்கி).
